title: Out of Africa: How Humans Spread Everywhere

cards.h: A small band of people walked out and changed the planet
cards.b:
Our species is only about 300,000 years old. Yet today we live on every continent. How did a creature from Africa end up in the Arctic and on remote islands?

The answer is a story of grass, coasts, ice and an astonishing amount of walking.

Fossils from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco date to about 300,000 years ago and show early Homo sapiens. Others have been found in Ethiopia (Omo Kibish, about 230,000 years ago).

We were not alone. Neanderthals lived in Europe and western Asia. Denisovans lived in Asia. Other human cousins lived on islands like Flores in Indonesia.

Most scientists think the main wave left Africa about 60,000 to 70,000 years ago. Some earlier trips happened too, and the dates are still debated. People probably followed coasts and rivers, not a single big march.

cards.h: We met our cousins, and had children
cards.b:
DNA from old bones shows that people outside Africa carry about 1 to 2 percent Neanderthal DNA. Some Asians and Pacific Islanders carry Denisovan DNA too. Tibetans carry a Denisovan gene that helps them live at high altitude.

So we did not just replace our cousins. We mixed with them.

Nobody knows for sure. Possible reasons: bigger social networks, better tools for trade and sharing, new hunting tools, or just bad luck in small, cold populations.

The Neanderthals were clever. They made fire, tools and perhaps jewellery. Historians and archaeologists still argue about the main cause.

When people reached Australia and the Americas, many giant animals vanished within thousands of years. Climate change played a part. Many experts think hunting did too. The balance is still debated.

This was the first time one species reshaped whole ecosystems.

cards.h: Out of Africa, or many places at once?
cards.b:
The 'multiregional' idea said humans evolved in several regions at the same time. DNA evidence has mostly settled it: all living people descend mainly from Africans. But the mixing with Neanderthals and Denisovans means the story is 'Out of Africa, plus some mixing'.

Also, one famous myth: 'Neanderthals were dim brutes'. Evidence says they were skilled and cared for their sick.

India's very early traces

At Attirampakkam, near Chennai, a 2018 study dated stone tools in one layer to about 385,000 years ago. Their makers were shifting from heavy hand-axes to smaller, finer blades, far earlier than once thought, and long before modern humans left Africa.

At Jwalapuram in Andhra Pradesh, Michael Petraglia's team found tools above and below the ash of the Toba supereruption of about 74,000 years ago. This suggests that people there survived a disaster that some scientists once linked to a worldwide human bottleneck.

A skull cap from Hathnora on the Narmada points to an even older, archaic human, though its date is debated.

Five things to remember

  1. Homo sapiens appeared in Africa about 300,000 years ago.
  2. The main spread beyond Africa was about 60,000-70,000 years ago.
  3. We interbred with Neanderthals and Denisovans.
  4. Reaching Australia and the Americas changed ecosystems.
  5. Dates and causes are still debated.

Think about it

  • Why do you think the coasts mattered so much for early travel?
  • What does mixing with other humans say about the word 'species'?

quiz.w: They date to about 300,000 years ago.

quiz.w: Known first from a finger bone in Denisova Cave, Siberia.
